reason: The sources provide robust, multi-source receipts explaining the 93-billion-light-year paradox and cosmic horizons.
story: If the universe is only 13.8 billion years old and nothing travels faster than light, you might assume our cosmic bubble is at most 27.6 billion light-years across. In reality, the observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years in diameter. This mind-bending gap is not an error or a breach of Einstein's cosmic speed limit. When the oldest light we can see was emitted 380,000 years after the Big Bang, its source was only about 40 million light-years away. But as those photons spent 13.8 billion years journeying toward Earth, the fabric of space itself expanded relentlessly behind and around them. Because space can stretch faster than the speed of light without breaking any local laws of physics, those ancient sources have been carried 46.5 billion light-years away from us today, creating an observable sphere containing trillions of receding galaxies.
angle: Although the universe is only 13.8 billion years old, the observable universe is 93 billion light-years wide because space itself expanded faster than light while photons traveled toward us.

claims.claim: The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old.
The observable universe has a diameter of roughly 92 to 93 billion light-years.
The radius, or comoving distance to the edge of the observable universe, is approximately 46 to 46.5 billion light-years.
In a static, non-expanding universe, light traveling for 13.8 billion years would span an observable radius of only 13.8 billion light-years.
The discrepancy between cosmic age and observable size is caused by the ongoing expansion and stretching of space during photon transit.
The speed-of-light limit applies to objects moving locally through space, not to the stretching rate of space itself.
Galaxies separated by vast cosmic distances can recede from one another faster than the speed of light without violating relativity.
The boundary of the observable universe is set by the particle horizon, marking the maximum distance from which signals have had time to reach us.
The cosmic microwave background radiation was emitted approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
The matter that emitted the cosmic microwave background was only roughly 40 to 42 million light-years away from our location at the time of emission.
The cosmic event horizon is currently located at a distance of about 16 to 16.6 billion light-years from Earth.
Events taking place today beyond the cosmic event horizon will emit light that will never reach Earth in the future.
Dark energy is responsible for driving the accelerated expansion of the universe.
The observable universe is estimated to contain up to 2 trillion galaxies.
The total number of stars in the observable universe is estimated to reach roughly 10^24.
Ordinary baryonic matter accounts for only about 4.8 to 5 percent of the universe's total energy density.
The entire universe beyond the observable bubble may be much larger or infinite in extent.
Hydrogen atoms represent the overwhelming majority of atomic matter in the universe.

disputed: Total galaxy count: older surveys based on Hubble data estimate 100 to 200 billion galaxies, whereas later models estimate up to 2 trillion galaxies; a script should state estimates range from hundreds of billions up to 2 trillion.

Exact diameter value: NASA sometimes rounds to 92 billion light-years in public educational explainers, while academic literature typically rounds to 93 billion light-years; a script should state 'between 92 and 93 billion light-years.'

Global geometry: CMB data indicates space is flat, but some gravitational lensing studies hint at a closed, spherical geometry; a script should attribute flatness as the consensus model while noting curvature remains under study.
